canonical_entities: LAUNCH EC2 INSTANCES ACROSS REGIONS VIA VPN
evidence.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
evidence.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: HARVESTED AWS IAM CREDENTIALS EXPOSED ON PUBLIC GITHUB REPOSITORIES
STEAL CLOUD ACCOUNT CREDENTIALS (AWS IAM CREDENTIALS EXPOSED IN PUBLIC REPOSITORIES)
evidence.text: Since at least December 2020, EleKtra-Leak—identified by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers William Gamazo and Nathaniel Quist—has programmatically harvested AWS IAM credentials exposed on public GitHub repositories within four minutes of exposure, exploiting blind spots in GitHub’s secret scanning and AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy; the adversary conducts account reconnaissance, blocklists victim accounts to deter analysis, configures security groups, then launches behind-VPN c5a.24xlarge EC2 instances from private, non-Marketplace AMIs to mine Monero, operating as many as 474 unique instances between August 30 and October 6, 2023, and fetching bespoke mining software via Google Drive. Evidence suggests overlap with a January 2021 cryptojacking campaign targeting unsecured Docker services using the same custom miner. Despite AWS’s two-minute quarantine response, the campaign maintains continuous fluctuations in compromised accounts, underscoring its rapid, large-scale cryptojacking impact. To mitigate risk, organizations must immediately revoke exposed API keys, remove them from GitHub, and audit repository cloning events for suspicious activity.
evidence.title: EleKtra-Leak Cryptojacking Attacks Exploit AWS IAM Credentials Exposed on GitHub

canonical_entities: PALO ALTO NETWORKS NGFW ADVANCED THREAT PREVENTION
evidence.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
evidence.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: PALO ALTO NETWORKS NGFW ADVANCED THREAT PREVENTION
evidence.text: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
evidence.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: MILITARY AND GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS IN HONG KONG, TAIWAN, VIETNAM, THE PHILIPPINES AND INDONESIA
evidence.text: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.
evidence.title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?
